newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Cardoso says slow reforms won't hurt Brazil.
newsitem.headline: Cardoso says slow reforms won't hurt Brazil.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said Brazil's economy was on a steady course and problems implementing structural reform did not pose a threat to the three-year-old plan that has slashed inflation.
"Despite the slow pace of reforms, the state has the means to keep inflation under control," Cardoso said in an interview with newspaper Gazeta Mercantil published Thursday.

The president also said a ballooning trade deficit -- expected to hit about $12 billion this year -- reflected Brazil's ongoing transformation into an open and competitive economy which would take "three or four years" to complete.
"During this period, even if there are deficits...we have the means for development and political stability and the ability to attract capital to finance the deficit," Cardoso told the newspaper.

After a succesful first two years, when Congress approved measures to open up the economy, Cardoso's reform program has come to a near standstill in the last 12 months with virtually no progress on key civil service and pension reforms.

On Wednesday, the government called off a latest attempt to vote on amendments to the civil service reform bill, fearing it did not have enough support to kill an opposition proposal that would allow public sector workers to keep their jobs for life.

In the Gazeta interview, the president said he would not resort to implementing reform by decree because previous presidents, most recently Fernando Collor de Melo, tried to take on Congress only to fall from power shortly afterwards.
"My aim is to give democracy roots," Cardoso said.

He said, however, that he would seek to reform electoral and political party rules to reduce the number of parties in Congress. Proposals for such changes are currently under study in the Senate, but are considered unlikely to be implemented in time for next year's elections.

In the short term, however, Cardoso cited the government's privatization program as an important tool for keeping its economic program on track and said the upcoming opening of Brazil's oil industry to private competition would also bring in foreign capital.
"We're starting to put a value on the state's assets. So we're not living under the threat of catastrophe, as long as we're competent," he told Gazeta.

Cardoso said that while he would like to see Brazilian gross domestic product growing by six or seven percent a year, compared with three percent expected for 1997, there was curently no scope for faster growth.

"The fundamental thing is to grow in the right direction, without provoking inflation," he said. "The general public does not know what GDP we're at. It wants to know if it's got work and food. The people who want to know about GDP are economists, principally from the opposition."

Asked about his expected bid to run for re-election next year, Cardoso was tightlipped, saying he was not yet a candidate. He also played down comments he made in another recent interview when he talked about closing ministries to save money, telling Gazeta that no closures were imminent.
